prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated with the trap perturbation cancelled, and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B036 with Katori and Ye. Having read the whole first-round exchange, I think the chair's central question, what the lattice clock added beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, has a concrete answer that can go into the rationale. The comb is a ruler for optical frequencies. The 2012 prize recognised control and readout of single ions. The lattice clock is a different invention: the magic-wavelength condition lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be held in a lattice with the trapping light shift cancelled, so the statistical power of many atoms is combined with the systematic control of an isolated atom. That combination is what took optical clocks to the 10^-18 level, and no earlier citation covers it. The result has been reproduced by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), which is the experimental verification I require. The consequences are already measured, not just promised: height-dependent redshift resolved over millimetre to centimetre scales and clock-based geodesy. The pairing is also the cleanest on the shortlist. Katori made the proposal and the first realisation, and Ye brought the system to record accuracy and stability. Johansson's move to B036 after reading the other ballots, and the fact that Eriksson and Mehlig both list it as their safe alternative, tell me this is the one configuration most of the room could accept without abandoning its own stated principles. I add that the comparison with B022 has sharpened my view: B022 is a real and original discovery, but its maturity case rests on a mechanism that is still open, and the committee's own criterion of being absolutely sure points to B036.
statement.case_against: The reservation all five supporters share remains: a sceptic can read the lattice clock as a very large improvement of a measurement technology that earlier prizes already honoured, and Kroll and Danielsson press this point from different sides. I do not think it is decisive, but I cannot say it is fully answered, because it depends on whether the committee accepts that an invention opening a new measurement regime counts as discovery under the will. The attribution is also not fully settled by the supplied names. Lemonde and collaborators, Takamoto and the RIKEN team, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made contributions that a two-name prize passes over, and our shared answers so far rest on recollection and not on the archival record. My own preferred topic of electron-optical aberration correction (B021) remains in my view the more transformative tool for materials science, but it has a single supporter, a priority question over Knut Urban that I cannot resolve, and I carry an obvious professional bias, so I do not advance it.

responses.point: Johansson moved B036 from seventh to first after reading the opening ballots and is the member who ranked it lowest; the chair asks whether Kroll's and Lindroth's answer settles his objection about the 2005 and 2012 prizes. He says the credit history is outside his specialty and that the redefinition of the second should not drive timing.
responses.response: I take his change of position as the strongest piece of evidence in the exchange, because it came from the member with the most doubt about overlap and was reached on device-physics grounds, not support counts. I would ask that his framing, the lattice clock as a controllable many-atom quantum system whose accuracy comes from the atom and not the trap, be used in the rationale, since it separates this from both earlier prizes more clearly than my own wording does. I agree with him on timing: the redefinition of the second is a metrology decision and the prize rests on the invention. His honest caveat on priority also stands, and neither of us can settle it from memory.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B036 first and calls it a new measurement technique opening new ways of observing nature, but lists priority among clock groups and the timing of the SI redefinition as open, and he declared a possible conflict on B007.
responses.response: I agree with his two-name reading and, on his open question of timing, I hold that waiting for the redefinition would delay the prize without improving the attribution or the science. On priority I can offer one thing in addition to recollection: the proposal of the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its first experimental realisation are the Tokyo contribution, while the accuracy and stability milestones that made it the leading standard are the JILA contribution, and those are the two roles the citation names. Whether Takamoto's part in the first realisation requires a different wording is the one point I would want checked against the primary papers before the vote, and I think we should say that openly in the discussion and not pretend the record is closed.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B022 and regards B036 as strong but incremental, a long refinement of metrology adjacent to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and asks whether the committee will recognise twisted bilayer graphene before the pairing mechanism is understood.
responses.response: I respect B022 and have it in my alternatives, and I agree that the magic-angle flat band and the observed phases are reproduced by many groups. On incremental, I disagree: a refinement leaves the underlying scheme intact, whereas the lattice clock changed the scheme, from a single trapped ion to many neutral atoms with the trap shift engineered away. I would also say that moving from eight years of reproduction to a prize for a theory-plus-experiment pair requires settling Cao's exclusion and the earlier moire band theory, which is the same archival check we lack for B036. Since you list B036 as your own safe alternative, the remaining objection I hear from you is about novelty, and I hope the rationale above addresses that.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022, separates the discovery of the flat band and its phases from the pairing mechanism, concedes that B036 is more mature and better settled, and says he would be comfortable moving to B036 if the committee weighs maturity above all.
responses.response: His separation of discovery from mechanism is reasonable, and I agree the cuprates and the quantum Hall effects were recognised before their mechanisms were understood. But the committee's practice, and the test I apply, is to be absolutely sure of the topic and of the people. For B022 that means being sure whether the prize is for the 2011 prediction, the 2018 experiments, or both, and how the exclusion of the first authors sits with the three-name limit. I find his concession on maturity decisive in practice: if his criterion is the maturity of the record, B036 meets it today, and I would ask him whether anything beyond maturity keeps him from joining it.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B012 and says he would accept B036 as the cleaner case, but regards the clock as an invention rather than a new observation of nature, and answered my question on why I ranked IceCube fifth by pointing to what blocks it.
responses.response: My own reason for ranking B012 fifth is the attribution, not the science: I accept that the diffuse flux is a first-rank discovery, but the credited pair do not represent the DUMAND, AMANDA and Baikal lineage or the analysts, and I would rather not carry a known allocation problem into a prize. On his invention-versus-discovery point, I would say the 10^-18 clock has already yielded measurements of nature, namely the gravitational redshift over millimetre heights and tightened bounds on drifts of constants, so it is not only a promise. I would keep B012 as an alternative and revisit it when independent source confirmations exist.

uncertainties: The archival priority record for lattice clocks: the exact roles of Katori, Takamoto, Lemonde, Ye and Ludlow, and whether a two-name credit survives a check against the primary papers.

Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct invention from the comb and ion-clock work, and not an extension of recognised metrology; I think it does, but the question is genuinely a matter of judgment.
For B022, whether the 2011 flat-band prediction and the 2018 experiments can be credited to three names without misattributing the experimental work, which is why I keep it only as an alternative.
For B021, the priority of Knut Urban relative to Rose, Haider and Krivanek, which I have not been able to resolve and which keeps me from advancing it.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1: since 2025 I am a Fellow of the University of Tokyo, where Hidetoshi Katori is based. I have no known collaboration with him, I do not believe this requires recusal, and I flag it so the committee can judge. I am a microscopist and so biased toward B021, which I am not advancing. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is a committee member; this does not bear on B036. I have no new conflicts after reading round 1.
